news.title: US Congressman puts Iran war, tariffs and healthcare on early House agenda
news.text: Digital Desk | Washington, Nov 23 (IANS) US House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries said that ending the Iran war, addressing President Donald Trump’s tariffs and reversing cuts to healthcare and food assistance would be early priorities for his party’s incoming House majority. Jeffries, the Democrats’ nominee to become speaker when the new Congress convenes in January, also proposed banning stock trading by members of Congress and exploring cooperation with Trump on healthcare, immigration and the cost of living. Speaking on CBS’s Face the Nation, he did not identify a single bill that Democrats would take up first. Instead, he outlined an agenda centred on affordability and accountability. “We have to drive down the high cost of living. Life is way too expensive,” Jeffries said. “There are far too many people who are working hard, they’re playing by the rules, they can’t thrive, and they can barely survive.” He put the war with Iran among the issues requiring early action. “We need to end this reckless and costly war of choice in Iran that has skyrocketed gas prices, food prices, and diesel prices. We need to reverse the Medicaid cuts. We need to restore SNAP benefits,” he said. Medicaid provides health coverage for eligible low-income people, while the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, known as SNAP, helps eligible households buy food. Jeffries also called for action on Trump’s tariffs, which he said had increased costs for Americans, and an extension of Affordable Care Act tax credits that help people pay health-insurance premiums. He did not identify particular tariff rates or countries whose exports would be affected by the proposed action. Asked whether Trump would sign legislation reversing parts of his signature tax-and-spending law, Jeffries rejected the suggestion that Democrats were preparing bills mainly to send a political message. “No, we’re committed to delivering the type of bold, dramatic, and meaningful change that the American people are demanding,” he said. Jeffries pointed to what he described as bipartisan House support earlier this year for extending the health-insurance tax credits. He said some Americans had experienced premium increases exceeding $1,000 a month. Asked whether Trump would veto a reversal of Medicaid cuts, he replied: “Listen, that remains to be seen.” Nevertheless, he identified affordability, healthcare and immigration as areas where Democrats could explore agreements with the president and Republicans. “We have a broken health care system. We need to fix it, and then make sure that we actually don’t simply return to the status quo, but we do much better than what currently exists,” he said. “And we need to fix our broken immigration system as well.” Jeffries did not set out specific immigration legislation during the interview. On healthcare, he proposed lowering the eligibility age for Medicare, the federal insurance programme principally serving older Americans, and expanding its coverage to include vision, hearing and dental care. He also called for ensuring that children and young Americans could afford to see a doctor. “That’s a place where we can explore coming together,” he said. On congressional accountability, Jeffries said Democrats would begin with their own institution by moving early in the new Congress to prohibit members from trading stocks. “We’ve got to clean up the mess in Washington. That means the Congress, that means the Supreme Court, and that also means with respect to the administration,” he said. Asked whether impeachment proceedings were an immediate plan, Jeffries declined to commit either way. “We haven’t ruled anything in, and we haven’t ruled anything out. We’re focused on actually delivering and keeping our commitment,” he said. Any investigations, he added, should follow the facts, apply the law and be guided by the Constitution.

news.title: Copper falls below $12,000 as doubts over AI spending deepen selloff
news.text:
Copper briefly sank below $12,000 a tonne on the London Metal Exchange, deepening a sharp selloff as doubts grow about demand from artificial intelligence.

The red metal tumbled 9 per cent last week as worries about the sustainability of AI spending fueled a global rush from risk. On Monday, copper opened with a gain of as much as 1.5 per cent before reversing direction and falling as much as 1.7 per cent. Analysts warned of more uncertainty.

Analysts divided over the outlook for copper

“Some copper bears are getting ready to exit,” said Gao Yin, an analyst at Shuohe Asset Management Co. “Others, however, think the whole AI narrative has fundamentally changed and want to stay aggressively short.”

Copper, used in the construction of data centers as well as energy infrastructure and wiring, soared to a record near $15,000 a tonne in September on AI enthusiasm and the prospect of US import tariffs on the metal. However, the Democratic Party’s sweep of the US midterm elections has fueled expectations for more scrutiny over the build-out, helping to send prices plunging this month.

Weak demand and AI spending concerns weigh on prices

The metal’s sharp slump last week — the third-biggest this decade — was emblematic of wider market turmoil as investors reconsidered prospects for spending on data centers and related infrastructure. Skeptics have also noted that AI is not likely to be a major driver of copper demand.

The mood turned markedly bearish at a major copper conference in Shanghai last week as industry participants reckoned with weak Chinese demand, a strong dollar and growing doubts over whether President Donald Trump would impose tariffs on refined metal this year.

US tariff uncertainty adds to market volatility

Expectations for import levies had drawn metal into the US and drained supplies elsewhere, buoying prices and contributing to a supply squeeze in China. By last week, traders were already preparing to ship copper out of US ports to relieve the supply pinch in Asia.

Copper fell 0.8 per cent at $12,069.50 a tonne on the LME as of 11:03 a.m. Shanghai time. Zinc dropped 0.7 per cent, while aluminum was up 0.1 per cent.

Published on November 23, 2026
news.summary: The metal’s latest decline reflects growing investor caution over data centre investments, Chinese consumption and the outlook for global copper supplies.

news.title: Microsoft defends overseas data centres after Trump threatens penalties
news.text: Digital Desk | Washington, Nov 23 (IANS) Microsoft President Brad Smith defended the need for data centres outside the United States after President Donald Trump threatened penalties on companies building them abroad, saying services used by businesses and consumers must operate close to their customers. Smith distinguished between facilities used to train the most advanced artificial intelligence models and those providing everyday cloud services, including video streaming, gaming and business applications. His remarks on CBS’s “Face the Nation” came as Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent acknowledged that he had not discussed the details of Trump’s proposal with the president. The debate has relevance for India, where Microsoft announced in December 2025 a $17.5 billion investment over 2026-2029 in cloud and AI infrastructure, skills and ongoing operations. Neither Smith nor Bessent identified India as a target of the proposed restrictions during their exchanges on the issue. Smith said there was room to discuss keeping the training of the most advanced AI models in the United States. But he cautioned against treating all data centres alike. “My sense is that the president is making an important point, but there's some critical nuance we need to think about as well,” he said. Most data centres, he said, provide cloud services rather than train advanced AI systems. Cloud computing allows customers to use software, storage and processing power over a network instead of maintaining all the equipment themselves. “They're cloud services to stream a video, play a video game, run your business. And those have to be located close to customers,” Smith said. He added that such services increasingly include AI features, including in business applications and video games. Using Finland as an example, Smith argued that facilities serving overseas customers could not simply be replaced by installations in the United States. “You can't support Helsinki from New Jersey any more than you can keep the lights on in Helsinki from an electricity power plant in New Jersey,” he said. “Those have to be located locally.” Trump at his Friday news conference said the United States would not allow data centres to move to other countries and threatened “tremendous penalties” against companies attempting to do so. Asked how that policy would work, Bessent said he had attended the news conference but had not spoken to Trump afterwards. “I haven't spoken to the president about that,” he said. Bessent interpreted Trump’s concern as preventing a major transfer of technology overseas. He drew a comparison with semiconductor manufacturing, arguing that dependence on production abroad had created a strategic vulnerability that the administration was trying to address. He also said technology companies needed to explain their plans better to Americans and rebuild trust with communities hosting data centres. Microsoft’s previously announced India programme illustrates the scale of its international commitments. The company said the $17.5 billion plan would build on an earlier $3 billion commitment and support expansion of its cloud and AI infrastructure alongside training and ongoing operations. That announcement included plans to expand data-centre regions in Chennai, Hyderabad and Pune. It was a multiyear investment commitment, not a statement that the entire amount had already been spent. Smith did not announce changes to those investments on Sunday. His central argument was that keeping advanced AI development in America and operating facilities near overseas customers were different questions requiring different policy decisions.

news.title: How much return can you expect?
news.text: In the case of fixed deposits, PPF, etc, nobody asks, “How much returns will I get?” That question is restricted to mutual funds — equity, BAF, equity savings, gold, etc. We know that it is IMPOSSIBLE to predict two-year returns, forget predicting 20-year returns!Whenever I do an article on returns and say 18%, or discuss what returns an investor can get, somebody will remark, “This is too high.” Of course, a few will say 18% is not possible, only 12% is possible, or something to that effect.We put a number because EXCEL cannot work with “I do not know” as an input. We assume that a Rs 5,000 per month SIP over 20 years at 12% will mean there will be Rs 55L in that fund. That is all. It is just proof that COMPOUNDING WORKS. Math needs an assumption, so we use that as an indicative number.It does not mean that you will get 12% or 18% in that fund. You may get 12% or 23% return. It is just an assumption. In real life, you will be watching it on a day-to-day basis. The important thing to learn is that you need to create funds that will remain untouched over really long periods of time. In real life, you can and perhaps will measure the returns regularly, so you do not need to play a guessing game today, at the beginning of your long journey.When a client asks an adviser, “What return will I get?”, the best thing is to ask the client to read this article. If you are an investor, save this article and read it again and again. Whenever you feel like asking this question, “kitna milega” — India’s favourite question!None of us know how much return we will get over four weeks, four years, or four decades. We just have no idea..However, you start a journey assuming that you need Rs 55 lakh in 20 years’ time. So you have to do a Rs 5,000 SIP for 20 years. If the return falls over two-three years, THE ONLY THING YOU CAN DO is increase the SIP amount that you are investing. If your adviser talks as though he controls everything, remember that HE CONTROLS NOTHING. Your eye should be on the target amount, that is all. So if you think that the ‘r’ (return) you are getting is not enough, try increasing the amount by a small amount. For you, reaching the figure of Rs 55L is more important than a theoretical discussion of ‘r’. Nobody knows what the “return” or “r” in the compounding formula will be — Donald Trump, Narendra Modi, Nirmala Sitharaman, or even Warren Buffett does not know how much return you will get over the next few weeks, months, years, or decades. We are all guessing.Every year, we will get a number. Say we get 8% return in the first year instead of 12%; we may not do anything. However, if we get 8% return for the first five years, we will take corrective action.We may increase the SIP amount to Rs 6,000 or whatever we can. Or, in a worst-case scenario, we may push the goal back by a year or two.We assume some numbers so that we can use Excel. We will monitor it continuously so that we can take corrective action if needed.The author is a Chartered accountant and CEO of subramoney.com .Follow The New Indian Express channel on WhatsApp Download the TNIE app to stay with us and follow the latest

news.title: Did Nick Bosa's Comments About Mexico City Fans Backfire?
news.text:
Nick Bosa walked out for warmups at Estadio Azteca on Sunday night and the stadium let him have it. Boos came first. Then came chants that were far from polite. The San Francisco 49ers defensive end had said something at practice in Colorado Springs, and Mexico City fans had clearly been saving their answer. Red jerseys filled the stands before the Minnesota Vikings game, and most of that crowd came to cheer the 49ers. Bosa turned out to be the lone exception, a star who gave a whole city one more reason to get loud.
What Nick Bosa Asked Of The Crowd
The trouble started midweek. Speaking after practice, Bosa looked back on the 2022 game at Estadio Azteca, where chanting rolled through the stadium from start to finish, the way it does at soccer matches across Mexico. He wanted fans to know when volume helps his team and when it hurts.
"I think we need some information given to the fans so they know when to cheer, because they just chant the whole time. No offense to them and their soccer cheering techniques, but if they can cheer when we're on defense, that would be great," he said.
TRENDING: #49ers DE Nick Bosa was heavily BOOED by fans in Mexico City as he entered the field. Bosa recently sparked backlash for saying Mexican fans needed guidance on when to cheer. Nick has also publicly supported Donald Trump & the MAGA movement. https://t.co/Ba7qal3LJS
— MLFootball (@MLFootball) November 23, 2026
Anyone who has tried to hear a snap count in a roaring stadium will get the point. Still, plenty of people in Mexico heard something else. Some Mexican media called the remarks condescending, and social media users urged fans to bring maximum noise on Sunday. That is a hard sell in a country where the 49ers have drawn cheers all three times they have played, and where the stands were a sea of red again this week.
A Quiet Season For Bosa Before The Mexico City Game
The boos landed on a player already wrestling with his own year. Bosa, 29, won Defensive Player of the Year honors in the past, but a calf injury has limited him to four games this season. He came into Sunday night with no sacks. He did not dodge the subject when reporters raised it.
"I don't think I'm playing my best football right now," Bosa said. "That's what gets me more so than the actual stats."
San Francisco arrived in Mexico with an 8-1 record, and Minnesota brought quarterback Kirk Cousins to the other sideline. Early live updates from the Mercury News showed tight end George Kittle scoring touchdowns to give the 49ers a lead. The same outlet also reported that offensive tackle Colton McKivitz suffered a serious leg injury during the first half.
news.summary: Nick Bosa of the San Francisco 49ers heard loud boos from Mexico City fans before facing the Minnesota Vikings. The cause was a comment about stadium chants, and now the defensive end needs a big game...

news.title: NATO-Like Guarantees For Ukraine? US Envoy Signals Possibility, But Questions Remain
news.text:
WASHINGTON -- US President Donald Trump may consider offering Ukraine security guarantees modeled on NATO's collective-defense commitments if he is convinced that the risk of another Russian invasion has been sufficiently reduced, special envoy Jared Kushner said.

In a lengthy post on X on November 22, Kushner described Russia's reported willingness to discuss such guarantees as "a major step forward" and a potential indication that Moscow was serious about peace.

But Moscow has publicly rejected NATO-like guarantees for Ukraine. Last week, Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Sergei Ryabkov called them unacceptable, raising questions about Kushner's characterization of Moscow's position.

Kushner also stopped short of announcing a US commitment, saying Trump would have to approve any proposed guarantee, subject to constitutional and congressional processes.

A US official told RFE/RL that Kushner's statement was significant because of his role in the negotiations. “The special envoy does not make statements without thought or understanding of all the parties involved, especially President Trump, who trusts him to negotiate,” the official said.

What Washington Is Considering

Kushner said a credible guarantee, backed by deterrence and arrangements to prevent military escalation, could “dramatically reduce the risk of another war.” He agreed with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy that guarantees must be "specific, credible, and clearly documented."

Kushner proposed a broader framework including permanent channels for consultation, crisis communication, military deconfliction, transparency, and reciprocal measures to reduce escalation.

The objective, he stated, should be a future in which “Ukraine is secure, Europe is stronger, Russia has confidence that NATO is not seeking confrontation, and NATO and its partners have confidence that Russia will respect the sovereignty and security of its neighbors.”

He stressed that Ukraine's security guarantees could not be finalized separately from the wider postwar European security architecture and that any arrangement must preserve the sovereignty and independent decision-making of participating countries.

Kushner also argued that lasting security required economic strength and a credible prosperity plan for Ukraine, including reforms to strengthen its institutions, economy, and self-reliance.

Citing Trump's conversation with leaders of the Coalition of the Willing, he said the hundreds of billions of dollars being spent on the war could instead be invested in jobs, economic growth, lower energy prices, and infrastructure.

He said Washington intended to work with Kyiv, European partners, and Moscow in the coming weeks to develop the proposed arrangements.

Zelenskyy Wants More

Kushner's post followed Zelenskyy's recent remarks after a meeting of the Coalition of the Willing in Berlin.

The Ukrainian president said full NATO membership remained the clearest security guarantee for his country and would also strengthen the alliance.

He questioned what an alternative "Article 5-like" arrangement would mean in practice, including which countries would participate, how they would defend Ukraine, and whether they would be prepared to repel another Russian attack.

The answers, he said, must be put in writing rather than left as general political assurances.

Zelenskyy also insisted that any guarantees must extend beyond Trump's presidency. Ukraine needs commitments not just for the next two years, he said, but for the long term. "That's not a strong peace. That's a two-year pause," he said.

Moscow's Rejection

Daniel Fried, a former US assistant secretary of state for Europe and Eurasia who served under seven administrations, told RFE/RL he saw no evidence that Moscow was prepared to discuss such guarantees.

"I would like to see the Russians say so. They have not," Fried said, pointing to Ryabkov's public remarks and Russia's continuing maximalist war aims. He cautioned against confusing a willingness to discuss a proposal with accepting it. "That 'discuss' is doing a lot of work," he said.

A genuine Article 5-like guarantee, Fried said, would mean the US and key European countries, potentially including members of the Coalition of the Willing, committing to treat an attack on Ukraine as an attack on them all.

"That would be a very big deal," he said. Such an arrangement could work, he added, but Russia would likely reject it. Full Ukrainian membership in NATO would be preferable for Kyiv, he said.

Fried questioned whether Kushner was outlining agreed US policy or attempting to win Trump's support for a proposal. "It would be far better if he had said Donald Trump supports this guarantee, subject to constitutional and congressional processes," Fried said.

"It almost appears that Jared Kushner is trying to walk a tightrope and create facts on the ground to present to Trump, rather than having a US government position," he added.

Pentagon’s NATO Vision

Fried also questioned how a potential US security commitment would fit with Pentagon policy chief Elbridge Colby's publicly stated priorities.

In a separate social media post on November 22, Colby described the transition to what he called "NATO 3.0," arguing that European allies should take the lead in conventional defense within the alliance.

Colby said US support for Ukraine should focus on helping it hold the front lines and conduct related mid-range strikes, which he described as the most effective way to strengthen Ukraine's defenses and create conditions for durable peace.

He said the transition toward European-led conventional defense was already producing results, with US allies demonstrating the industrial capacity and political will to assume greater responsibility.

Fried said those priorities raised questions about how Washington could simultaneously move toward reducing its conventional military role in Europe while taking on significant new security obligations to Ukraine.

"If we are about to undertake additional security obligations, an Article 5-like guarantee for Ukraine, I want to know what additional forces will be required, and how will this be done?" he said.

Fried also warned that negotiations over reciprocal measures to reduce tensions could give Moscow an opportunity to introduce demands of its own.

Despite his reservations, Fried said Kushner's post was sufficiently forward-leaning to merit serious attention. "I had been dismissive of Kushner's talk about Article 5-like guarantees, but this tweet is sufficiently forward-leaning that I'm taking it seriously," he said.

Guarantees Must Be Credible

Kristina Kvien, a former director for Europe at the US National Security Council and former charge d'affaires at the US Embassy in Ukraine, was more skeptical.

Kvien, now president of the Pacific Council on International Policy, told RFE/RL that the phrase "Article 5-like guarantees" was too vague without clearly defined and enforceable mechanisms.

She also questioned Kushner's assertion that Russia was comfortable discussing the concept, particularly given Ryabkov's rejection.

Even a written commitment, she said, would be only as reliable as Washington's willingness to honor it. "The Trump administration has not built the trust necessary to ensure the commitment will be kept," Kvien said.

"The most credible security guarantee for Ukraine is full NATO membership," she added.

Kushner, meanwhile, said the proposed security arrangements, combined with economic recovery and a broader European security framework, were intended to lay the groundwork for a lasting settlement.

He described the ultimate goal as "a sovereign, secure, prosperous and free Ukraine, a stronger and more stable Europe, and a lasting peace built on arrangements that make another war far less likely."

“Nothing is agreed until it is agreed," he emphasized. "But the willingness to engage on these historic questions creates an important opportunity to stop the bloodshed.”
news.summary: US President Donald Trump may consider offering Ukraine security guarantees modeled on NATO's collective-defense commitments if he is convinced that the risk of another Russian invasion has been sufficiently reduced, special envoy Jared Kushner said on November 22.
news.author: Alex Raufoglu

news.title: US Vice President Vance declines to say he would have ordered Iran strikes
news.text:
US Vice President JD Vance on ​Friday declined to say whether he would have authorised strikes on Iran to prevent the country from developing a nuclear weapon, ‌sidestepping President Donald Trump's calls for him to say the attacks were necessary and that he would carry them out again.

Speaking at a White House press conference alongside Trump, Vance said the decision to attack Iran in February was Trump's call, "and my job is to support the president of the United States."

The answer underscored the delicate balancing act the ​vice president and his party face as the Iran conflict creates domestic political challenges.

In a blunt midterm election postmortem, Vance blamed the war for ​Republicans' historic losses and called for the US to exit the conflict. Many viewed his statement, posted on social ⁠media, as a break with Trump as the vice president considers a 2028 White House bid.

"The reason we lost is the war," Vance wrote. "The president ​himself said so last night. If you'd like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, ​then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay."

Trump on Friday said he was not unhappy with Vance's conclusion, but said it lacked a crucial element: an acknowledgment that the strikes were necessary and that Vance would make the same decision.

"People that work for me, they have a right to their opinion," Trump said. "But I say, ​I know the Iranians, and, frankly, they're crazy."

When asked later in the press conference if the war was worth Republicans' steep congressional losses, Vance did not explicitly ​endorse the operation.

"What I've said is the goal of keeping Iran from getting a nuclear weapon is absolutely what we need to be doing," Vance said. "It's the biggest ‌state sponsor ⁠of terrorism. If they had a nuclear weapon, they would use it as leverage, or, God forbid, they would attack and kill thousands, hundreds of thousands, potentially of innocent people.

"And I think the president is the one who makes the decision, and the president has said he would do it again. And my view is that my goal is and my job is to support the president of the United States."

Vance has long opposed the war and ​acted as Washington's main emissary for peace ​talks, brokering a short-lived provisional ⁠truce over the summer that quickly fell apart.

In recent weeks, he sent personal correspondence to hardliners in Tehran to restart negotiations. But Trump called off the engagements shortly after Vance published his post-campaign assessment, telling the vice president to focus ​on domestic policy.

“We don’t need a deal with Iran,” Trump wrote on social media, announcing his direction to Vance. “Those ​days have long ⁠since passed.”

Trump returned on Thursday from a four-day diplomatic trip through Asia, which culminated in an unprecedented trilateral meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin.

Trump faced criticism for meeting — and exchanging warm greetings — with both leaders. He hugged Xi after landing in China and called Putin "my friend."

White House officials cast ⁠the meeting ​as a show of mature statesmanship, arguing that Trump's relationships, even with US adversaries, displayed Washington's ​global strength.

Vance, who remained in Washington, was the trip's chief cheerleader. He quipped during the press conference that remaining stateside during Trump's mission was like the 1990 family comedy film "Home Alone."

"It's ​amazing what's possible when you give diplomacy a real chance," he wrote Thursday on social media.
news.summary: US Vice President JD Vance on ​Friday declined to say whether he would have authorised strikes on Iran to prevent the country from developing a nuclear weapon, ‌sidestepping President Donald Trump's calls for him to say the attacks were necessary and that he would carry them out again.

news.title: Egypt sees path to Iran deal, cites $20 billion Suez Canal losses
news.text: Digital Desk | Washington, Nov 23 (IANS) Egypt sees a path to an agreement between the United States and Iran and is working with regional partners to rebuild trust, Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty said on Sunday, warning that continued conflict was imposing heavy economic costs across the Middle East. Speaking on CNN’s “Fareed Zakaria GPS,” Abdelatty said regional tensions had cost the Suez Canal $20 billion in revenue and driven up the prices of oil, gas and wheat. “Egypt is paying a heavy price,” he said. The Suez Canal connects the Mediterranean and Red seas, providing a shipping route between Europe and Asia without the longer journey around southern Africa. Abdelatty said Egypt was coordinating daily with Qatar, to bring Washington and Tehran back to negotiations. “I believe that there is a possibility for dialog, for reaching a deal, for reaching a compromise,” he said. A lack of mutual trust remained an obstacle, he added. The countries involved in the diplomatic effort were working on confidence-building measures to help move negotiations forward. Asked directly whether he saw a path to a deal, he replied: “Yes. And we are hopeful for that.” He argued that both the United States and Iran had an interest in reaching an accommodation and warned that a military approach could bring further devastation to countries across the region. His comments indicated continued diplomatic efforts, but he did not announce an agreement, a date for renewed talks or commitments accepted by either side. Describing the economic impact, Abdelatty said the consequences extended beyond the Gulf countries to other regional economies. For Egypt, higher food and energy prices were compounding the loss of canal earnings. The problem was not simply whether essential goods were available, he said, but whether people could afford them. Those pressures were among the reasons Cairo was promoting diplomacy and peaceful solutions. In a separate exchange on Gaza, Abdelatty urged a return to President Donald Trump’s peace plan, calling it “the only game in town now.” He said Egypt, Turkey and Qatar had persuaded Palestinian factions, including Hamas, to agree to hand over heavy and light weapons. He accused Israel of failing to respond positively. That was the Egyptian minister’s account of the mediation effort; he did not say that the weapons handover had been completed. Abdelatty also accused Israel of obstructing humanitarian assistance, saying the first phase of the peace plan had not been fully implemented and the stated minimum of 600 aid trucks entering Gaza had not been achieved.

news.title: Trump's Thanksgiving turkeys arrive at luxury DC hotel as Americans vote on their names
news.text: Talk about talking turkey. Two feathered VIPs have checked into one of Washington's most luxurious hotels, complete with plush beds, a red-carpet welcome and a crowd of eager photographers, ahead of President Donald Trump's annual Thanksgiving turkey pardon at the White House. The presidential hopefuls arrived Sunday at the historic Willard InterContinental Washington, D.C., where they were photographed strutting across a red carpet, posing for pictures and standing atop the hotel's beds before their big day on the South Lawn. THE PENNSYLVANIA FARM BEHIND A WHITE HOUSE THANKSGIVING TURKEY TRADITION The U.S. Department of Agriculture celebrated their arrival on X, announcing a "SPECIAL DELIVERY TO WASHINGTON, D.C.!" and describing the birds as "two VERY special guests" receiving the presidential treatment. Photographs shared by the USDA, credited to the White House and National Turkey Federation, showed the plump white birds making their grand entrance before an audience of hotel guests and photographers. One turkey was even pictured riding through the hotel's ornate hallways inside a travel crate perched on a brass luggage cart. The pair appeared equally comfortable with the accommodations, with one bird spreading its feathers atop a neatly made bed while its companion stood nearby. But before the turkeys meet the commander in chief, Americans have been invited to settle a pressing matter of national importance: What should they be called? SOCIAL MEDIA USERS ARE EATING HUGE AMOUNTS OF CARROTS AND SHRIMP FOR A NATURAL TAN The White House launched an online contest offering three possible combinations: "Commander & Chief," "Freedom & Feathers," and "Honey & Ham." Voting on the names closed Sunday at 5 p.m. ET, with the winning pair expected to be announced before a second round of voting opens Monday at 8 a.m. That final vote will determine which turkey receives the official ceremonial pardon. The birds, raised by American turkey farmers Scott and Becky Rightsell at Deans Gap Farm in West Virginia, have already received their own playful presidential biographies. Both hatched July 15, but their tastes apparently differ. According to the White House, one enjoys Golden Delicious apples and scenic country drives, while the other prefers Dr Pepper and dreams of vacationing in Aggieland. The pair was selected from a larger flock based on appearance and temperament, according to West Virginia Gov. Patrick Morrisey's office. Their preparations included getting accustomed to crowds, camera lights and noise. And for Americans who cannot get enough turkey-related excitement, the White House has unveiled "Gobble Getaway," an online game challenging players to help a turkey dodge a chef armed with a net and roasting pan while making its way across the South Lawn to the pardon podium. The annual Thanksgiving tradition dates back to 1947, when the National Turkey Federation first presented a holiday bird to President Harry Truman. Bush established the formal presidential turkey pardon in 1989. Trump and first lady Melania Trump are scheduled to participate in this year's ceremony on Tuesday, Nov. 24, at 2 p.m. ET on the White House South Lawn. Although the public gets to vote on which turkey receives the ceremonial pardon, both birds are traditionally spared the Thanksgiving dinner table. news.title: US intelligence chief predicts more tech outages as systems undergo upgrades
news.text: Americans should expect more technology outages and disruptions as companies and government agencies replace aging systems, the top US intelligence official said on Sunday."And as part of that ongoing upgrade, we are going to have glitches, gaps, interruptions in service," Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton told CNN's "State of the Union" program. "That is going to happen."Clayton was interviewed on Sunday morning news programs days after President Donald Trump attributed a recent spate of technology failures to upgrades of companies' technology systems. Clayton said the upgrades were necessary to improve performance and cybersecurity as technological advances strain older systems.A string of technology failures this month disrupted critical US systems, including a nationwide halt to air travel, a Microsoft outage that hit email services, a technical glitch that affected several major banks and a temporary disruption to the National Security Agency's network.Speaking on the ABC program "This Week," Clayton reiterated his previous statements that those outages were not the result of coordinated or state-sponsored actions, attributing them to technical upgrades.Clayton declined to discuss specifics of separate reports of cyberattacks on the FBI and Department of Agriculture, saying he expects investigators to provide answers "in due course."
